**HBM is the large warehouse; on-chip storage is the small workbench.** A tensor can fit in device memory while being far too large for shared memory or registers. Efficient kernels move a tile onto the chip, reuse it, and write only the needed result back. Shared memory is explicitly coordinated by the program; caches manage reuse differently. [1](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/)

Consider three elementwise transformations of a million-element float32 tensor. If each runs separately and writes its result to device memory, each stage moves approximately four megabytes in and four megabytes out: about 24 MB across three stages, ignoring caching. An ideal fused kernel reads the initial four megabytes, computes all three operations locally, and writes the final four megabytes: about 8 MB.

The arithmetic did not disappear. The savings came from avoiding intermediate trips to the warehouse. This is especially valuable when those trips cost more time than the operations themselves.

**The workbench can overflow.** A fused kernel that keeps too many temporary values may use excessive registers or shared memory, reducing how many work groups run concurrently. Spilling registers can bring memory traffic back. Hence “fuse everything” is not a sound rule. Use a profiler to compare traffic, occupancy, and elapsed time. Capacity and aggregate bandwidth numbers depend on the device and measurement convention; compare actual bottlenecks rather than treating all on-chip storage as one uniform memory.

**Technical details and references.**

HBM provides large device-wide storage; registers and shared memory provide much smaller, faster on-chip storage close to execution units. Shared memory is explicitly managed, while caches have hardware-managed behavior. Capacity and bandwidth figures depend on GPU, allocation, and how aggregate bandwidth is measured. [1](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/)

Kernel fusion keeps intermediate values in registers/shared memory instead of writing them to HBM and reading them in another kernel. For a sequence of elementwise operations, one input read and one final output write can replace several full-tensor passes. Fusion also reduces launches.

Too much fusion can increase register pressure, reduce occupancy, or force spills back to memory. Synchronization boundaries and incompatible tiling can prevent profitable fusion. Measure memory traffic and execution time rather than assuming every fused graph is faster.
